redcross_kit.title: What Do You Need In a Survival Kit

kit-phases.summary: Ready.gov recommends a basic kit with several days of water and food, a flashlight, a battery or hand-crank radio, extra batteries and a first-aid kit. Building it in phases spreads the cost.

family-plan.summary: A family emergency plan writes down where you will meet, how you will reach each other, and who your out-of-area contact is. It costs nothing to make.

evacuation-routes.summary: Know more than one way out of your neighbourhood and practise it, so you are not deciding under pressure.

transportation-plan.summary: If you do not drive or may not have a vehicle available, arrange in advance who will drive you or which transit or paratransit service you would use.

alerts-on.summary: Wireless Emergency Alerts and NOAA Weather Radio warn you about hazards in your area. Turning alerts on is free and takes a minute.

meds-7day.summary: Keep at least a 7-day supply of daily medications, with a written list of what each person takes. Talk to your doctor or pharmacist about building and rotating that supply.

backup-power.summary: Equipment such as oxygen concentrators, CPAP machines, dialysis equipment and powered wheelchairs stops working in an outage. Plan a backup power source and know where you would go if the power stays off.

infant-feeding-kit.summary: CDC's emergency infant-feeding checklist covers what to store for breastfed and formula-fed infants, including clean water, feeding supplies and a way to clean them.

evacuation-helper.summary: If you would need help to leave, agree in advance with a specific person who will come for you, and have a backup person.

pet-kit-lodging.summary: The Red Cross recommends a go-kit for each pet and identifying pet-friendly lodging ahead of time, because many emergency shelters cannot take pets.
